# The research wrote each life in its own words from the Wikipedia article and a second reference. It copied no sentence.

text: King of France from 1180, Philip spent the years around 1200 grinding down the Angevin realm, signing the Treaty of Le Goulet in 1200 and seizing Normandy by 1204. In the same years his rejection of his Danish queen Ingeborg brought a papal interdict on France. Cold, patient and calculating rather than chivalrous, he won the name Augustus for the lands he added to the crown.

Philip II's heir married Blanche of Castile in 1200 as part of the peace with King John. Later, invited by rebel barons, he invaded England in 1216 and was proclaimed king in London before the cause collapsed. Called the Lion, he reigned only three years, dying of dysentery in 1226 after a crusade in the south, and was remembered for his piety and loyalty to his wife.

A daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile, Blanche was picked by her grandmother Eleanor of Aquitaine and married to the future Louis VIII in 1200, aged twelve. She became one of the most capable rulers of her age, twice governing France as regent. A famous story says that when Philip II refused money for Louis's English war, she threatened to pawn her children to raise it.

A French knight of enormous strength in the service of Philip II, William crossed swords with Richard the Lionheart more than once, and his quarrel with Richard began at a tournament rather than a mock fight at Messina in 1190. In the wars with the Angevins around 1200 he was one of the king's best fighters. At Bouvines in 1214 he rescued the unhorsed Philip and twice grabbed Emperor Otto by the neck during his retreat.

A Knight Hospitaller from Pont-Sainte-Maxence, Brother Guerin became Philip II's keeper of the seals from 1201. Elected bishop of Senlis in 1213, he still rode to war and drew up the French battle line at Bouvines in 1214. Later chancellor of France from 1223, he was a quiet, tireless administrator who ran the realm from behind the throne.

Count of Dreux and Braine and a grandson of Louis VI, Robert was a cousin and staunch ally of Philip II. He fought at Acre and Arsuf on the Third Crusade and then in the long war for Normandy, where he grabbed the castle of Nonancourt while Richard I sat captive in Germany. He later joined the Albigensian Crusade and fought for his king at Bouvines in 1214.

A baron of the Ile-de-France with a claim to the earldom of Leicester, Simon joined the Fourth Crusade but walked out when it turned on the Christian city of Zara in 1202. From 1209 he led the Albigensian Crusade, crushing Peter II of Aragon at Muret in 1213. Austere, devout and merciless, he was killed at the siege of Toulouse on 25 June 1218 by a stone from a siege engine.

Youngest son of Henry II, John became king of England in 1199 on the death of his brother Richard. Within five years he had lost Normandy and most of his French lands to Philip II, and the suspected murder of his nephew Arthur blackened his name. Clever but suspicious and vindictive, he squeezed his barons for money until they forced Magna Carta on him in 1215.

A younger son with no inheritance, William made his name as an almost unbeatable tournament champion and served four Angevin kings. Marriage to the heiress Isabel de Clare made him Earl of Pembroke, and around 1200 he was one of King John's chief magnates. At about seventy he became regent for the boy Henry III and won the Battle of Lincoln, remembered as the very model of a loyal knight.

A clerk trained in the royal household, Hubert went on the Third Crusade with Richard I and helped raise his ransom. As Archbishop of Canterbury from 1193 he also ran the government as justiciar, then served King John as chancellor from 1199 until his death in 1205. A gifted, worldly administrator, he made the royal chancery keep regular copies of its letters, a habit that shaped English record keeping.

A minor Norfolk landowner who rose through King John's household, Hubert was chamberlain around 1200 and briefly the keeper of the captive Prince Arthur. He held Chinon against the French in 1205 and Dover against Prince Louis in 1216, then won the sea fight off Sandwich in 1217. A chronicle tale, later used by Shakespeare, says he refused to have Arthur blinded.

Duchess of Aquitaine in her own right and queen first of France and then of England, Eleanor was nearly eighty in 1200. Even so she crossed the Pyrenees to choose her granddaughter Blanche as bride for the French heir, and in 1202 she held out at Mirebeau until her son John rescued her. Proud, bold and politically shrewd, she died at Fontevraud in 1204.

Younger son of the conqueror of Meath, Hugh overthrew John de Courcy in Ulster in the years 1203 to 1204 and was rewarded by King John with the earldom of Ulster. He fell out with John in 1210 and fled when the king came to Ireland in force. A restless adventurer, he recovered his Irish lands in the 1220s after years of exile.

A grandson of Henry I through an illegitimate line, Meiler came to Ireland with the first Cambro-Norman invaders and carved out lands in Leinster. He was justiciar of Ireland from about 1198 to 1208, the king's chief officer there, and quarrelled hard with William Marshal over Leinster. His kinsman Gerald of Wales wrote about the early campaigns in Ireland.

An illegitimate son of Henry II and half-brother of King John, William became Earl of Salisbury by marriage in 1196. He stayed loyal to John through most of the reign, destroying a French fleet at Damme in 1213 before being captured at Bouvines in 1214. His name, Long Sword, is usually taken to refer to his great height and the outsized weapons he carried.

An illegitimate son of Henry II, Geoffrey was made Archbishop of York by Richard I, perhaps to keep him out of the succession. Around 1200 he was locked in disputes with his own cathedral chapter and with King John. Stubborn and quarrelsome, he defied John's taxes in 1207, fled into exile and died in Normandy in 1212.

Count of Toulouse from 1194, Raymond ruled a rich land where the Cathar faith spread under his tolerant eye. Excommunicated and blamed for the murder of a papal legate in 1208, he was publicly scourged at Saint-Gilles before facing Simon de Montfort's crusade. A slippery survivor who married five times, he was beaten at Muret in 1213 but retook Toulouse in 1217.

Viscount of Carcassonne, Beziers, Albi and the Razes, Raymond Roger was a young lord who sheltered Cathars among his subjects. When the Albigensian Crusade came in 1209, Beziers was sacked and Carcassonne fell after a short siege. Taken prisoner when he came out to bargain, he died in his own dungeon on 10 November 1209 at twenty-four, and Occitan memory made him a martyred hero.

Count of Foix from 1188, Raymond-Roger accompanied Philip II to the Third Crusade and fought at the siege of Acre in 1190. His sister Esclarmonde was a leading Cathar, and he became one of the hardest fighters against Simon de Montfort, standing with Peter II at Muret in 1213. He argued his own case before the pope at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, and crusader chroniclers painted him as a brutal enemy of the Church.

Count of Comminges in the Pyrenean foothills from 1176, Bernard was a close ally of the counts of Toulouse. His tangled marriages drew papal anger: he wed Maria of Montpellier in 1197 and cast her off, after which she married Peter II of Aragon. In the Albigensian Crusade he fought against Simon de Montfort, standing with the southern lords at Muret in 1213, and died in 1225.

King of Aragon and Count of Barcelona from 1196, Peter was crowned in Rome by Innocent III in 1204, earning the name the Catholic. He married Maria of Montpellier, fought beside Castile at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, and then marched north to shield his Occitan vassals. He was killed at Muret on 12 September 1213 while charging into Montfort's knights.

A younger son of Alfonso II of Aragon, Alfonso was made Count of Provence as a small boy and in 1193 married Gersenda, heiress of Forcalquier. Around 1200 he ruled Provence for the House of Barcelona, a cultured court full of troubadours. He died at Palermo in February 1209 while escorting his sister Constance to marry Frederick II.

Guillem Ramon of the Montcada family, lords of Tortosa, held the hereditary office of seneschal of Barcelona. He fought beside Peter II at the sieges of Castielfabib and Ademuz in 1212 and that year was betrothed to the king's natural daughter Constance, marrying her in 1222. From 1218 he served as procurator of the realm for the young James I, and he died in 1228.

Son of Count Sancho of Roussillon and grandson of Ramon Berenguer IV, Nuño was a teenager in 1200 at the court of his cousin Peter II. He took over Roussillon and Cerdagne around 1212, invested by Peter II that year, but reached Muret too late to save the king in 1213. He then helped govern for the boy James I.

King of Castile from the age of three, Alfonso married Eleanor, daughter of Henry II of England. Crushed by the Almohads at Alarcos in 1195, he spent the next years rebuilding and in 1200 took Alava and Gipuzkoa from Navarre. His great revenge came at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, the victory that made him a hero of the Reconquista.

Lord of Biscay and head of the Haro family, Diego was one of the greatest magnates of Castile and often royal standard-bearer for Alfonso VIII. Proud and touchy, he broke with the king more than once around 1200 and went off to serve Navarre and Leon. Reconciled, he led the vanguard at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, and later writers called him both the Good and the Bad.

Born in Navarre and schooled at Bologna and Paris, Rodrigo became Archbishop of Toledo on 27 February 1209 and the leading churchman of Castile. He preached the crusade that ended at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 and rode with the army there. A scholar as much as a statesman, he wrote a great Latin history of Spain and laid the first stone of the Gothic cathedral of Toledo on 14 August 1226.

A son of the powerful House of Lara, Alvaro was royal standard-bearer to Alfonso VIII and was made a count in 1214. He then seized the regency for the boy king Henry I from Berengaria and ruled Castile until Henry was killed by a falling roof tile in 1217 while in his care. Ambitious and scheming, he took up arms against Berengaria and her son and died in 1218.

King of Leon from 1188, Alfonso summoned the Cortes that year with representatives from the cities, often called the first parliament in Europe. Around 1200 he was at odds with Castile and the pope, whose objections ended his marriage to Berenguela. Later the founder of the University of Salamanca in 1218 and conqueror of Merida, he was nicknamed the Slobberer, said to foam at the mouth in his rages.

Eldest child of Alfonso VIII, Berengaria married her cousin Alfonso IX of Leon in 1197 to seal a peace, until Innocent III voided the marriage in 1204. She then guarded the interests of her children from Castile. In 1217 she inherited the Castilian crown and at once handed it to her son Ferdinand III, guiding policy for decades, a patient and astute queen called the Great.

Head of the Castro family and heir to the royal Infantazgo of Leon, Pedro served Ferdinand II and then Alfonso IX as chief steward. A bitter enemy of the rival Lara clan, he broke with Castile and even fought on the Almohad side at Alarcos in 1195. Around 1200 he was a leading Leonese baron, but he ended his life in exile in Morocco on 18 August 1214, still an outcast.

Second king of Portugal from 1185, Sancho took Silves with crusader help in 1189 but lost it to the Almohads two years later. Around 1200 he worked to fill his empty frontier lands with settlers and new towns, earning the name the Populator, while quarrelling with his bishops. He also wrote verse, and a love song in Galician-Portuguese is attributed to him.

Heir of Sancho I, Afonso was gravely ill as a youth around 1200 and was later called the Fat. As king from 1211 he issued Portugal's first written general laws at the cortes of Coimbra and fought his sisters over the castles their father had left them. Sickly but stubborn, he checked the power of the nobles and the Church and died excommunicated in 1223.

Grandson and namesake of the great Gonçalo Mendes the Good, he became head of the Sousa house in 1192 and that same year chief steward of the court of Sancho I. Around 1200 he was the king's leading noble, and in that year he set up the boundary stones when Sancho endowed the shrine of Saint Senhorinha. Proud and independent, he made the Sousas perhaps the strongest family in Portugal.

Fourth Almohad caliph from 1199, Muhammad al-Nasir inherited a vast empire from his father al-Mansur, the victor of Alarcos. He took Majorca from the Banu Ghaniya and won back Ifriqiya, leaving it under the governor whose line became the Hafsids. His invasion of Castile ended in disaster at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, and legend tells of slaves chained around his tent there.

Abu Said Uthman ibn Jami came from a family of Andalusi administrators who served the Almohad court in Marrakesh. He was vizier to the caliph Muhammad al-Nasir from about 1205 and steered much of the daily business of the empire. After the defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 he helped arrange the succession of the next caliph, but he later lost power and was killed in exile.

Abd al-Wahid was a son of Abu Hafs Umar, the Hintata chief who had been one of Ibn Tumart's first companions. A leading Almohad general, he defeated enemy forces in a battle in October 1205, and in 1207 the caliph left him in Tunis as governor of Ifriqiya with unusually wide powers. A steady and trusted frontier lord, he founded the Hafsid line that would later rule Tunisia for three centuries and died on 25 February 1221.

Abd al-Wahid al-Marrakushi was born in Marrakesh in 1185 and studied in Fez and in al-Andalus, mixing with scholars close to the Almohad court. Around 1200 he was a young student of law and letters. Later he travelled east and finished al-Mujib, a history of the Maghreb, in 1224, a work lively with personal anecdote and frank judgements of the caliphs.

Yahya ibn Ishaq ibn Ghaniya led the Banu Ghaniya, the last Almoravid loyalists, who had sailed from Majorca to wage war on the Almohads in Ifriqiya. Taking command around 1188 after his brother Ali died, he seized Mahdia and on 14 December 1203 Tunis itself. Defeated in 1205, he never gave up, raiding from the desert edges for more than thirty years and earning a name as the most stubborn rebel of the Maghreb.

Sharaf al-Din Qaraqush was a mamluk of Armenian origin who served Saladin's nephew Taqi al-Din and was sent west in the early 1170s. He carved out a domain around Tripoli and the Tunisian Jarid and fought the Almohads. He allied with the Banu Ghaniya but was not a member of that family. He quarreled with Yahya ibn Ghaniya and was defeated and executed by him in 1212.

Philip of Swabia, youngest son of Frederick Barbarossa, was first trained for the church before becoming duke of Swabia. After his brother Henry VI died, the Hohenstaufen party elected him king in 1198 against the Welf Otto IV, and he slowly won the upper hand despite papal hostility. Gentle and courteous, praised by the poet Walther von der Vogelweide, he was murdered at Bamberg on June 21, 1208 by Otto of Wittelsbach.

Henry of Kalden was a ministerial of the Pappenheim family who served as imperial marshal to Henry VI and led his armies in Sicily. Around 1200 he was one of Philip of Swabia's chief commanders in the war against Otto IV. Utterly loyal to the Hohenstaufen, after Philip's murder in 1208 he hunted down the assassin Otto of Wittelsbach and killed him in March 1209.

Conrad of Querfurt was imperial chancellor to Henry VI and then to Philip of Swabia, and bishop first of Hildesheim and then of Wurzburg. He went on the crusade of 1197 and wrote a vivid letter about the wonders of Italy. Ambitious and worldly, he moved between sees without papal leave until Innocent III forced him to submit, changed sides in 1201, and was murdered by vassals in Wurzburg in 1202.

Ludolf of Kroppenstedt was archbishop of Magdeburg from 1192 to 1205 and one of the senior princes of the Saxon church. He backed Philip of Swabia in the disputed election of 1198 and hosted the king's splendid crown-wearing at Magdeburg at Christmas. He held firm for the Hohenstaufen despite papal pressure on the German bishops, and he died in August 1205.

Otto IV, son of Henry the Lion and nephew of Richard the Lionheart, grew up at the Angevin court and was made count of Poitou. In 1198 the Welf party elected him German king against Philip of Swabia, starting ten years of civil war. Tall, brave and headstrong, he was crowned emperor in 1209, broke with the pope over Sicily, and lost everything after the defeat at Bouvines in 1214.

Adolf of Altena was archbishop of Cologne from 1193 and the leading kingmaker of the Rhineland. In 1198 he engineered the election of Otto IV and crowned him at Aachen. He later crowned Philip of Swabia instead, for which the pope deposed him in 1205. A calculating politician who traded his vote for advantage, he spent years trying to regain his see and died in 1220.

Henry the Elder of Brunswick was the eldest son of Henry the Lion and brother of Otto IV. His marriage to Agnes of Hohenstaufen in 1193 made him count palatine of the Rhine from 1195, and he joined the crusade of 1197. He supported Otto after 1198 but went over to Philip of Swabia in 1204, a flexible broker between the two great houses who outlived both rival kings.

Henry I, called the Courageous, was the first duke of Brabant and ruled from Leuven for over fifty years. In the throne dispute after 1198 he backed Otto IV, then Philip of Swabia, then Otto again, and finally Frederick II, always for a price. He founded many towns and fought for Otto at Bouvines in 1214. His shifting loyalties made him one of the great opportunists of the age.

Frederick II, son of Henry VI and Constance of Sicily, was born at Jesi in 1194 and crowned king of Sicily as a small child in 1198. Around 1200 he was an orphan in Palermo, a ward of Pope Innocent III fought over by German captains and Sicilian barons. He grew into a brilliant, restless emperor who spoke several languages, wrote on falconry and was called the wonder of the world.

Markward of Annweiler was an imperial ministerial who rose to be seneschal of Henry VI and margrave of Ancona. After Henry's death he claimed the regency of Sicily for the young Frederick and fought the pope's men across the kingdom. Innocent III called him another Saladin and preached a crusade against him. A hard and capable soldier, he fell ill and died in September 1202 at Patti.

Walter of Palearia was bishop of Troia and chancellor of the Kingdom of Sicily under Henry VI and Constance. During the minority of Frederick II he was a leading member of the regency council, bargaining in turn with the pope, Markward of Annweiler and other German captains. A slippery and ambitious prelate, he became bishop of Catania in 1208 but later fell from favour with the young king.

Diepold of Schweinspeunt was a Bavarian ministerial whom Henry VI made count of Acerra in southern Italy. After 1197 he fought on for himself and the Hohenstaufen cause, killing Walter of Brienne in an ambush at Sarno in June 1205 and later contending for Palermo and the boy king. Otto IV made him duke of Spoleto in 1209. A tireless raider, he left a trail of sacked towns recorded by Richard of San Germano.

Ottokar I of the Premyslid dynasty secured Bohemia in 1197 and was crowned king by Philip of Swabia in 1198. He changed sides between Philip and Otto IV whenever it served him, and in 1212 Frederick II confirmed the royal title as hereditary in the Golden Bull of Sicily. A cunning and tenacious politician, he raised Bohemia to a kingdom that would weigh heavily in the Empire.

Vladislaus Henry was a younger brother of Ottokar I. Elected duke of Bohemia in 1197, he gave up the throne to Ottokar after only months, and he ruled Moravia as margrave from then until his death in 1222. Peaceable and loyal, he avoided civil war with his brother, and their partnership let the Premyslids speak with one voice in the conflicts of the Empire.

Born Lotario dei Conti di Segni, Innocent III became pope in 1198 at about 37 and was the most powerful pontiff of the Middle Ages. He claimed authority over all Christian kings, used interdicts to bend rulers such as Philip II of France and King John, launched the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade, and crowned his work with the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215. Brilliant, legalistic and tireless, he saw himself as Christ's vicar set above nations.

Riccardo was the elder brother of Pope Innocent III and the chief winner from his nepotism. With papal backing he gathered castles and estates in Latium, and the huge Torre dei Conti in Rome is linked to his family. In 1208 his brother invested him with the county of Sora on the Sicilian border, taken from imperial partisans. A grasping baron rather than a churchman, he made the Conti a lasting power in Roman politics.

Peter of Capua, of a noble family of Amalfi, was a Paris-trained theologian and a cardinal from February 1193. As papal legate in France he laid the kingdom under interdict in January 1200 to force Philip II back to his rejected wife Ingeborg. He then served as legate to the Fourth Crusade and the Latin East, and he brought the relics of Saint Andrew from Constantinople to Amalfi, where the cathedral received them on 8 May 1208. He was admired as a brilliant preacher and scholar.

Ugolino dei Conti, a kinsman of Innocent III, was made a cardinal in 1198 and became one of the curia's sharpest lawyers and diplomats. He was the friend and protector of Francis of Assisi and helped shape the Franciscan rule. Elected pope as Gregory IX in 1227, already very old, he issued the Decretals, set up the papal Inquisition and fought the emperor Frederick II, whom he excommunicated more than once. He was famed for his iron will.

Enrico Dandolo was elected doge of Venice in 1192 when already in his eighties and nearly blind. He struck the bargain that bent the Fourth Crusade to Venice's profit, used the crusaders to retake Zadar in 1202, and led the assault on Constantinople in 1204, standing armed at the prow of his galley under the banner of Saint Mark. Shrewd, pious and amazingly vigorous for his age, he died in Constantinople in 1205 and was buried in Hagia Sophia.

Ranieri was the son of Doge Enrico Dandolo and governed Venice as vice-doge while his father was away on the Fourth Crusade. After the conquest he worked to secure Venice's share of the Byzantine lands, above all Crete, which the Genoese privateer Enrico Pescatore had seized. He led the first Venetian attack on the island in 1207 and was killed in the long war with Genoa for Crete. His daughter Anna later married the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanjić.

Pietro Ziani, son of the rich doge Sebastiano Ziani, had been a sea captain in his youth and belonged to one of the wealthiest families in Venice. He took part in the Fourth Crusade and was elected doge in 1205 after Enrico Dandolo's death. He organised Venice's new holdings in Crete, Corfu and Constantinople, made treaties with Greek rulers and fought off Padua. Calm and businesslike, he gave up the office in 1229 and died soon after.

Tommaso Morosini, a Venetian noble cleric who was still only a subdeacon, was chosen by the Venetian clergy of Hagia Sophia as the first Latin Patriarch of Constantinople in 1204. Innocent III first condemned the election as uncanonical, then confirmed him and had him ordained priest and bishop in quick order. As patriarch he was accused of filling posts with Venetians and quarrelled with the emperor, French clergy and papal legates until his death in 1211.

Baldwin IX, Count of Flanders and Hainaut, was a pious and popular young prince who took the cross in 1200 and became one of the leaders of the Fourth Crusade. After the fall of Constantinople in 1204 the crusaders chose him as the first Latin emperor on April 13. Within a year he was defeated and captured by the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan at Adrianople in 1205 and died in captivity. His mysterious end let an impostor named Bertrand de Rains claim his name in Flanders in 1225.

Henry, younger brother of Baldwin of Flanders, fought with distinction in the Fourth Crusade and became regent and then emperor of the Latin Empire after Baldwin was captured. Crowned in 1206, he defended the young state against Bulgarians and Nicaeans and won over many Greek nobles by treating them fairly. A brave soldier and a tolerant, practical ruler, he is often judged the ablest of all the Latin emperors of Constantinople.

Conon de Béthune was a knight of Artois and a celebrated trouvère whose songs mix courtly love with crusading zeal. On the Fourth Crusade his eloquence made him the crusaders' spokesman in their dealings with the Byzantine court. He stayed in the Latin Empire as one of its leading barons and twice served as regent of Constantinople, dying there in 1219. Villehardouin praised him as a good knight and a wise, fine speaker.

Canute VI, son of Valdemar the Great, was king of Denmark from 1182. Guided by Archbishop Absalon, he refused homage to the emperor Frederick Barbarossa and extended Danish power over Pomerania and Mecklenburg and, in 1201, Holstein. Contemporaries describe him as earnest and deeply religious, a quiet king overshadowed by his ministers and his warlike brother Valdemar. He died childless in November 1202, aged thirty-eight or thirty-nine.

Valdemar, younger brother of Canute VI, was Duke of Schleswig in 1200 and fought for Holstein before succeeding as king in 1202. Called Sejr, the Victorious, he built a Baltic empire reaching Estonia, where legend says the Danish flag fell from heaven at the battle of Lyndanisse in 1219. Kidnapped by a German vassal in 1223, he lost most of his conquests, and spent his later years giving Denmark the Code of Jutland.

Absalon, of the mighty Hvide clan, was bishop of Roskilde and archbishop of Lund, foster-brother and chief adviser of Valdemar the Great and then of Canute VI. A warrior prelate, he led fleets against Wendish pirates and destroyed the pagan temple at Arkona on Rugen in 1168 or 1169 and fortified the harbour village that became Copenhagen. He joined church reform to fierce loyalty to the crown. In 1200 he was old and near his end, and he died on 21 March 1201.

Anders Sunesen, nephew of Absalon, studied in Paris, Bologna and Oxford before serving as royal chancellor, and succeeded his uncle as Archbishop of Lund in 1201. A learned lawyer and poet, he put the Scanian Law into Latin, wrote the long theological poem Hexaëmeron and promoted crusades in the eastern Baltic. Later legend, modeled on the story of Moses in Exodus, says that at Lyndanisse in 1219 he prayed on a hill with raised arms while the Danes fought below.

Born in Murcia in al-Andalus, Ibn ʿArabī was a Sufi mystic, poet and philosopher who sought out the spiritual masters of Spain and North Africa. Around 1200 he left the West for good and reached Mecca in 1202, where he began his vast Meccan Revelations. Later honoured as the Greatest Master, he taught that all things are manifestations of one divine reality. His visions and daring ideas made him both revered and fiercely controversial.

Walther von der Vogelweide was the greatest German lyric poet of the Middle Ages, a travelling singer who lived on the favour of princes. Linked above all with the Babenberg court of Vienna, he left it around 1198 and took up the cause of Philip of Swabia, writing the first political poetry in German. His love songs crown the Minnesang tradition. Proud and sharp-tongued, he mocked the pope and stingy patrons alike until Frederick II gave him a small fief.

Geoffrey of Villehardouin, Marshal of Champagne, was a seasoned knight and negotiator. In 1201 he was one of the envoys who agreed the fateful shipping treaty with Venice, and he stayed at the heart of the Fourth Crusade's councils through the capture of Constantinople. His eyewitness account, On the Conquest of Constantinople, is the oldest surviving French prose history. He wrote as a loyal, level-headed insider who defended the choices of the leaders.

Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat, was a veteran soldier and a generous patron of troubadours, chosen leader of the Fourth Crusade in 1201. Passed over for the imperial crown in 1204, he took Thessalonica and central Greece as his kingdom instead, driving out Leo Sgouros. He was killed in 1207 in a Bulgarian ambush in the Rhodope mountains, and his head was sent to Tsar Kaloyan. Courtly, ambitious and brave, he was praised in the songs of Raimbaut de Vaqueiras.

Francis was the pleasure-loving son of a rich cloth merchant of Assisi; in 1202 he fought for his city against Perugia and spent a year as a prisoner. Illness and spiritual crises turned him to radical poverty. He rebuilt ruined chapels, cared for lepers and gathered brothers whose way of life Innocent III approved around 1209. Joyful, gentle and theatrical, he preached to birds and in 1223 staged the first Christmas crib at Greccio, and was said to bear the stigmata.

Dominic de Guzman, a Castilian canon of Osma, travelled north with his bishop Diego on a royal embassy to Denmark around 1203 and saw the Cathar faith spreading in Languedoc. He stayed to preach against it in poverty, debating the heretics openly rather than relying on force. In 1216 the pope approved his Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, devoted to study and preaching. Austere and tireless, he was known for spending whole nights in prayer.

Leonardo of Pisa, son of a Pisan merchant official, grew up partly at Bugia in North Africa, where he learned the Hindu-Arabic numerals and Arab mathematics. In 1202 he published the Liber Abaci, which taught Europe to reckon with the new numerals and posed the rabbit problem behind the Fibonacci sequence. He later won the attention of the emperor Frederick II. Many count him the finest mathematician of medieval Europe.

Walter III, Count of Brienne in Champagne, married Elvira, daughter of the late King Tancred of Sicily, and set out to win her inheritance. Backed by Innocent III, he entered southern Italy in 1201 with a small army, won battles at Capua and Cannae and became prince of Taranto. He fought the German captain Diepold for years. In June 1205 Diepold ambushed him at Sarno, and he died of his wounds three days later.
